medium.resumo: I wasn’t even looking for this story
medium.conteudo_html:
I wasn’t even looking for this story

I’d deleted Instagram for months. This week I reinstalled it out of pure boredom, and the first thing in my feed wasn’t a reel or a meme. It was a brother and sister hugging on the Nasdaq floor in New York.

Dario and Daniela Amodei. The co-founders of Anthropic, the company behind Claude. On November 19 they rang the opening bell as their company pulled off the biggest IPO in history: about $81.3 billion raised, more than SpaceX managed in June.

I scrolled past. Then I scrolled back. I vaguely remembered these two used to work at OpenAI, and one question wouldn’t leave me alone: how do two people walk out of the hottest AI company on earth and, five years later, beat it to Wall Street? So I went down the rabbit hole. Here’s what I found.

They didn’t leave OpenAI for the money

Long before ChatGPT was a thing, the Amodeis were senior people at OpenAI. Dario ran research. Daniela ran safety and policy. Both worked on GPT-3, the model that quietly set up everything that came after.

Then, at the end of 2020, Dario left. Daniela and a group of colleagues followed. The reason most often reported: they were uneasy about where OpenAI was heading after Microsoft’s money came in, and felt safety was sliding down the priority list. There are also reports of friction with Sam Altman and Greg Brockman.

What gets me is the timing. They left before ChatGPT launched. Before the hype. Before anyone knew how big this would get. They walked away from the rocket right before it took off, betting they could build it more carefully somewhere else.

In 2021 they started Anthropic with a few other OpenAI alumni, including Jared Kaplan, Tom Brown, Chris Olah, Sam McCandlish, Jack Clark and Ben Mann. I’ve always found sibling founders fascinating, and these two make sense together. Dario is the scientist. Daniela is the builder who turns research into an actual company. Daniela once told Time that the two of them have felt aligned since they were kids. Watching that hug on my screen, I believed it.

The growth numbers broke my brain

Anthropic started life as a safety-first research lab. It’s set up as a public benefit corporation, and a big chunk of its research is about figuring out what is actually going on inside AI models. Time compared it to a brain scan for AI.

But this is where I had to reread things twice. According to the company’s IPO filing, revenue was $41 million in 2023. Then $386 million in 2024. Then about $4.6 billion in 2025. And in just the first six months of 2026? $16.3 billion.

From $41 million a year to $16 billion in half a year, in roughly three years. I genuinely can’t think of a growth curve like it.And it’s mostly businesses paying, not people like me chatting with a bot. More than 1,900 companies paid Anthropic at least $1 million each over the past year.

The valuation chased the revenue. $61.5 billion in March 2025. $183 billion that September. $965 billion in a private round this year. And now a public company worth more than a trillion dollars.

IPO week was a rollercoaster

Here’s how the week played out.

On Wednesday, Anthropic priced its shares at $83, above the $70 to $78 range it had been pitching, and sold more shares than originally planned. The ticker is ANT.

On Thursday, the stock opened at $111.50, a 34% jump. For a few hours the company was worth around $2 trillion.By Thursday’s close it had cooled to $97.17. Still up 17%.On Friday it dropped almost 9% to $88.65.Honestly, that two-day swing says more about the market’s mood than any headline. Euphoria at the open, nerves by Friday.

One thing that surprised me: Amazon and Google each own stakes in Anthropic worth over $100 billion, and Google, Microsoft, Nvidia and AMD put in another $26 billion together at the IPO. Basically all of Big Tech has skin in this game. And OpenAI, the company the siblings walked out of, is expected to go public in 2027.

So is this all a bubble?

This is the part I actually care about. After reading both sides, my honest answer is: I don’t know, and I don’t think anyone does yet.

What worries me. Anthropic has committed to roughly $895 billion in spending, mostly on computing power. That’s way more than it earns. It lost over $8 billion on operations in 2025, and nearly a quarter of that year’s revenue came from just two customers. Finance professor Aswath Damodaran argued these AI giants are being priced on hype metrics rather than properly valued. Some investors even worry that being public will push Anthropic to chase revenue over safety, which is pretty much the exact thing the siblings left OpenAI over. That irony is hard to ignore.

What makes me think it’s not 2000 all over again. This isn’t a dot-com with no revenue. Real businesses are paying real money, and fast. The operating loss in the first half of 2026 was just $693 million on $16.3 billion of revenue. That scary $80 billion “net loss” headline you might have seen is mostly an accounting effect from convertible bonds going up in value, not cash being burned. And reports say the company has started posting operating profits on an adjusted basis.

Where I’ve landed. One business professor put it in a way that stuck with me: the real question isn’t whether there’s a bubble, it’s which AI companies survive it. The dot-com crash wiped out a lot of companies, but Amazon and Google came out the other side. Both things can be true at once. An overheated market and a genuinely world-changing technology.

What I’m taking away

Five years ago, two siblings quit one of the most important AI labs on earth because they thought it was moving too fast. This week, their company became the biggest IPO ever.

The people most worried about AI are now among its biggest winners. I can’t decide if that’s reassuring or unsettling. Maybe both.

Whether ANT becomes the Amazon of this era or the face of a bubble won’t be decided in one wild week. But I’ll be watching: OpenAI’s IPO, the next earnings report, and probably way too many Instagram posts arguing about all of it.

Guess I’m keeping the app.So what do you think, bubble or the real thing? Tell me in the comments.

Not investment advice. Just someone who fell down a rabbit hole.

medium.titulo: AI in Software Development: Why the Real Win Is System Thinking, Not Faster Code Generation
medium.resumo: > “The fastest team is not the one that writes the most code with AI. It is the one that makes the fewest wrong decisions before the code…
medium.conteudo_html:
> “The fastest team is not the one that writes the most code with AI. It is the one that makes the fewest wrong decisions before the code exists.”

1. The real problem is not code generation. It is decision quality.

Most teams are using AI exactly the wrong way. They ask for a feature, get a few hundred lines of code back, and call it progress.

The problem is that AI writes code fast in the absence of constraints, trade-offs, and failure semantics.

This is not productivity. It is optimistic overconfidence.

2. AI is useful in every phase of delivery — but its value changes by phase

The strongest teams do not think of AI as a code generator. They think of it as a tool that helps at different points in the software lifecycle.

Requirements

AI is useful for:

- Turning vague requests into structured specs

- Extracting constraints from tickets, docs, and incident notes

- Identifying missing edge cases

- Converting business intent into testable acceptance criteria

Design

AI helps with:

- Comparing architecture options

- Spotting unclear ownership boundaries

- Identifying missing failure modes

- Turning vague ideas into ADRs and design briefs

Implementation

AI helps with:

- Scaffolding boilerplate

- Generating repetitive code

- Writing initial tests

- Suggesting refactor candidates

Validation

AI helps with:

- Generating test ideas

- Reviewing edge cases

- Identifying risky assumptions

- Summarizing logs, traces, and failures

The key point is simple: AI is not equally valuable in all phases.

That is where system thinking matters. Not syntax.

3. The dangerous pattern: faster code, worse judgment

A bad AI-assisted workflow looks like this:

// Bad: AI writes a feature from a loose ticket without system constraints
export async function createOrder(input: OrderInput) {
  const order = await repo.insert({ …input, status: 'created' });
  await paymentClient.charge(input.amount);
  await emailService.send(order.userId, 'Order confirmed');
  return order;
}

This looks reasonable. It is also dangerously incomplete.

It ignores:

- Duplicate requests

- Payment retries

- Out-of-stock edges

- Idempotency requirements

- Partial failure semantics

- What happens if email or payment fails after the order is created

The problem is not that the code is “wrong.” The problem is that the code assumes the system is simpler than it really is.

A better version is driven by explicit constraints:

// Good: AI works inside a defined contract and failure model
export async function createOrder(input: OrderInput): Promise<Result<Order, OrderError>> {
  const idempotencyKey = input.idempotencyKey;
  if (!isValidOrder(input)) {
    return { ok: false, error: 'INVALID_ORDER' };
  }
  const existing = await orderRepo.findByIdempotencyKey(idempotencyKey);
  if (existing) {
    return { ok: true, value: existing };
  }
  const order = await orderService.create(input);
  const paymentResult = await paymentGateway.authorize(order.total);
  if (!paymentResult.ok) {
    await orderService.markFailed(order.id, paymentResult.error);
    return { ok: false, error: 'PAYMENT_FAILED' };
  }
  await orderService.confirm(order.id);
  return { ok: true, value: order };
}

It is code written under a clearer contract. The distinction matters.

4. Where AI creates technical debt

AI creates technical debt in a very specific way: it compresses the time between idea and implementation so much that the team skips the expensive thinking phase.

This happens when:

- Requirements are vague

- Constraints are not explicit

- Failure behaviors are never modeled

- Trade-offs are not captured

- The team treats generated code as “good enough” without validation

Common patterns:

- Abstraction without a real repeated need

- Hidden coupling between service layers

- State stored in too many places

- Weak retry logic and no idempotency guarantees

- Tests that validate happy path and ignore edge conditions

- Architecture that is “pretty” but operationally unstable

AI is not the cause of bad software. Bad process is. But AI makes bad process faster.

5. Human-in-the-loop is not a slowdown. It is the safety mechanism.

A strong AI workflow is not “AI does everything.”

It is “AI proposes, humans constrain, systems validate, and people decide.”

The best teams use AI in a loop like this:

1. Define the problem clearly

2. Ask AI for options and trade-offs

3. Review assumptions and failure modes

4. Choose a direction with explicit reasoning

5. Generate implementation under that direction

6. Validate behavior with tests and real user flows

7. Keep a record of the decision in ADRs or design notes

This is what makes AI productive instead of reckless.

6. The real AI advantage: reducing uncertainty earlier

A good engineering team does not optimize for writing more code. It optimizes for reducing uncertainty earlier.

AI helps in a few very concrete ways:

- It surfaces missing requirements before implementation starts

- Itchallenges bad assumptions before they become infrastructure

- Itcreates candidate designs faster than an engineer can on a blank page

- Itaccelerates review when the system is not obvious

- Ithelps teams compare options based on trade-offs, not vibes

That is faster learning. And faster learning is what actually increases delivery speed in a safe way.

7. Final takeaway

It will make them faster. The win is better system thinking earlier.

The teams that ship reliably in the AI era will be the ones that use AI to:

- Clarify intent

- Challenge assumptions

- Improve verification

- Capture trade-offs

- Keep responsibility with humans

That is how you turn AI from a code amplifier into a design multiplier.

💡 Hint/Takeaway: If your AI workflow starts with “generate code,” it is already too late. Start with spec, constraints, failure modes, and review. Then let AI accelerate the rest.

medium.titulo: We Spent $300,000 Modernizing Our Backend. The Business Got Slower
medium.resumo: Why expensive microservices migrations, cloud transformations, and Java modernization projects fail to deliver business value and what…
medium.conteudo_html:
Why expensive microservices migrations, cloud transformations, and Java modernization projects fail to deliver business value and what engineering leaders should measure before approving another rewrite.

Why backend modernization projects fail, how microservices migrations increase costs, and what CTOs should measure before rewriting legacy systems.

A company approves a $300,000 backend modernization project because its legacy application has become difficult to maintain. The engineering team promises faster deployments, better scalability, cleaner architecture, and a platform that will support the next five years of growth. Six months later, the monolith has been divided into twelve microservices, the infrastructure runs on Kubernetes, and the engineering team has replaced several outdated components with modern frameworks. The migration is declared successful because the new services are running in production and the old deployment pipeline has finally been retired.

Then the CFO asks an uncomfortable question: “Why does it take longer to launch a new feature now?”

The engineering team has a reasonable explanation. A feature that previously required changes inside one application now touches four services, two event contracts, and a shared authentication layer. Developers spend additional time coordinating deployments, debugging distributed transactions, and maintaining infrastructure that didn’t exist before the migration. The architecture looks more modern, but the company has traded one category of technical debt for another. This is a hypothetical scenario, but the failure pattern is familiar across software organizations. Modernization projects often begin with legitimate engineering problems and gradually become technology replacement programs whose success is measured by migration progress rather than business outcomes. Teams celebrate removing the last legacy component without demonstrating that the replacement system is cheaper to operate, easier to change, or more reliable under real production conditions.

The Legacy System Wasn’t Beautiful. It Was Also Paying the Bills.

Legacy applications rarely survive for years because everyone loves their architecture. They survive because they contain business rules, operational knowledge, and years of fixes for unusual situations that nobody remembers until those situations happen again. A financial system might contain complex payment allocation logic, historical reconciliation behavior, and transaction validation rules that evolved through hundreds of production incidents. An order management application may encode exceptions for international shipping, partial fulfillment, customer-specific pricing, and integrations with systems that were never documented properly. From an engineering perspective, the code can look terrible. From a business perspective, the application may be processing millions of dollars in transactions every month with acceptable reliability. These two observations can be true simultaneously, and ignoring either one creates expensive decisions.

When a company decides to rewrite such a system, it is taking responsibility for rediscovering all the behavior embedded in the original implementation. Some of that behavior is unnecessary complexity, but some represents business requirements that were never written down. A clean architecture diagram cannot tell engineers which historical edge cases are still commercially important. The first mistake is assuming that old code is automatically expensive and new code is automatically valuable. The relevant question is how much the existing system costs the company through maintenance effort, delivery delays, operational risk, and missed business opportunities. If those costs cannot be measured, leadership has no reliable way to evaluate whether a proposed rewrite is justified.

Microservices Can Make a Small Engineering Organization Less Productive

Microservices architecture solves specific organizational and technical problems. It can allow independently owned services to scale, deploy, and evolve without requiring coordinated releases across an entire application. Those benefits become valuable when the organization has clear service boundaries, sufficient operational maturity, and workloads that justify independent scaling or deployment. But splitting a monolith does not automatically create those conditions.

Imagine a backend team with eight engineers maintaining a Spring Boot application. The application contains customer management, orders, payments, inventory, and reporting modules. Deployments are occasionally difficult because the codebase has accumulated dependencies between business domains. Leadership decides to divide the application into separate services, expecting engineers to become more productive once each domain has its own deployment pipeline.

The migration introduces service discovery, distributed tracing, API gateways, asynchronous messaging, centralized configuration, additional databases, and Kubernetes deployment manifests. A simple feature that previously involved one database transaction now requires coordinating state across several services. Engineers begin spending more time on network failures, backward compatibility, message ordering, and environment configuration. The organization has gained deployment independence in theory, but feature delivery still requires coordination because the business boundaries were never properly separated. The services remain coupled through synchronous API calls, shared assumptions about data, and workflows that span multiple teams.

The company has distributed its code without meaningfully distributing its ownership. This distinction matters because microservices are an organizational architecture as much as a technical one. Without independent responsibilities and stable contracts, the migration can increase operational complexity while preserving the original development bottlenecks.

The Hidden Cost of a Modern Cloud Architecture

Modern cloud infrastructure makes it possible to deploy sophisticated distributed systems with relatively little upfront hardware investment. Kubernetes, managed databases, message brokers, observability platforms, and automated deployment pipelines can provide capabilities that would have required substantial infrastructure teams in earlier years. But each additional component creates ongoing operational responsibilities.

A company migrating from a single application to multiple services may need additional compute capacity, separate database instances, load balancers, logging pipelines, monitoring infrastructure, network controls, and more sophisticated deployment automation. Some of these costs scale with usage, while others remain relatively fixed even when business traffic is low. The engineering cost can be even more significant. Developers need to understand how services communicate, how failures propagate, how distributed traces are interpreted, and how to diagnose problems that cross application boundaries. Production incidents may involve several teams because no single service owns the entire business workflow.

Consider an illustrative annual cost comparison for a relatively small system.

Illustrative annual operating costs

Existing architecture
Application infrastructure:       $18,000
Database and backups:             $12,000
Monitoring and logging:            $6,000
Total:                            $36,000

Proposed distributed architecture
Application infrastructure:       $42,000
Databases and backups:            $24,000
Networking and gateways:          $12,000
Monitoring and logging:           $18,000
Additional platform operations:   $48,000
Total:                           $144,000

Illustrative annual increase:    $108,000

These numbers are hypothetical and should not be treated as representative industry benchmarks. Actual costs depend on workload, deployment design, cloud provider, operational practices, and whether existing staff can absorb additional responsibilities. The example illustrates why infrastructure expenditure and operational labor need to be included in a modernization business case. A migration that improves scalability may be financially worthwhile if it enables substantial growth or prevents costly failures. But if the company’s transaction volume is stable and its main problem is slow feature delivery, introducing a distributed platform may solve the wrong problem.

Java Modernization Is More Than Upgrading Spring Boot

Java modernization projects often begin with an apparently straightforward objective: upgrade an old Java application to a supported JDK and Spring Boot version. The motivation can be entirely legitimate, especially when unsupported dependencies introduce security exposure or prevent the organization from receiving important fixes.

The difficulty appears when the migration encounters assumptions embedded throughout the application. An older Spring application may depend on deprecated APIs, outdated Hibernate behavior, custom authentication filters, legacy serialization formats, and database queries that rely on implementation-specific behavior. Upgrading the framework can expose transaction boundary problems, dependency incompatibilities, or changes in how persistence operations are executed.

A technically successful compilation doesn’t establish that the application behaves correctly under production workloads. For example, an application may pass functional tests after a migration while experiencing increased database connection pressure because transaction lifetimes or query behavior changed. A new connection pool configuration may work in staging but become problematic when multiple application replicas compete for a limited number of PostgreSQL connections.

Suppose the database permits 200 connections and the application runs eight replicas, each configured with a maximum pool size of 30. The theoretical application-side maximum is 240 connections before accounting for administrative connections, background jobs, or other clients. The configuration may remain harmless during light traffic but become dangerous when concurrent demand increases. The arithmetic is simple. The operational consequences are not. A reliable modernization plan should evaluate connection pool sizing, transaction duration, query performance, thread utilization, garbage collection behavior, dependency compatibility, and rollback requirements. It should also verify business-critical workflows against known expected behavior, particularly where the application handles payments, inventory, customer records, or other financially significant operations.

The Database Is Where Many Rewrites Become Expensive

Application code is often easier to replace than the data model it depends on. A legacy database may contain years of accumulated business rules expressed through constraints, triggers, stored procedures, historical schemas, and relationships that are poorly understood outside the original engineering team. During a microservices migration, developers may propose giving each service its own database. This can improve ownership and reduce coupling when boundaries are well designed. However, it also changes how the organization handles transactions that previously relied on a single relational database.

Consider a payment workflow that updates a payment record, adjusts an outstanding balance, and creates an accounting entry within one database transaction. Moving those responsibilities into separate services introduces coordination and recovery requirements. A failure after the payment service commits but before the accounting service processes its event can leave the business workflow temporarily incomplete. The architecture needs to represent that state explicitly. It may require an outbox, durable messaging, idempotent consumers, compensating actions, and reconciliation processes that detect transactions exceeding acceptable completion windows. Financial correctness cannot depend on the assumption that every asynchronous operation eventually succeeds without intervention.

Data migration introduces another category of risk. Backfills can create significant database load, historical records may violate new constraints, and dual-write strategies can produce inconsistent state when one destination succeeds and another fails. Teams need validation procedures, migration checkpoints, and a rollback or forward-recovery strategy appropriate to the changes being made. A modernization project that treats database migration as a secondary implementation detail is taking an unnecessary risk with the company’s most valuable operational asset.

Why Feature Delivery Gets Slower After a Rewrite

One of the most revealing modernization metrics is lead time for change. It measures how long work takes to move from a committed code change to production, although organizations should also examine the broader time from business request to usable functionality.

If the architecture is genuinely improving developer productivity, the organization should eventually observe measurable improvements in delivery speed, deployment reliability, or the cost of making changes. Those improvements may take time because migrations introduce temporary overhead, but leadership should define expectations before the project begins. Consider a hypothetical team that previously delivered a moderate business feature in eight working days. After moving to microservices, similar features require twelve days because developers must coordinate API changes, update event contracts, provision environments, and validate cross-service behavior. The team now has more deployment pipelines, but each business feature touches more independent components.

The migration has increased technical flexibility in certain areas while reducing delivery efficiency in others.

This outcome can be corrected if the underlying problem is poor service boundaries or excessive coordination. However, it requires examining actual development workflows rather than assuming that more independent deployments automatically produce faster business delivery. Engineering leaders should measure change lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate, recovery time, and the engineering effort required for representative features. These measurements need context because comparing fundamentally different projects can produce misleading conclusions.

A successful modernization should make the organization demonstrably better at delivering and operating software. Completing the migration is only one milestone in that process.

The Architecture Review That Should Happen Before the Rewrite

Before approving a major modernization investment, I would examine the current system through the lens of business constraints and production evidence. The objective would be to identify which architectural limitations actually create financial or operational consequences. First, I would review recent production incidents and recurring engineering bottlenecks. Which failures are caused by the existing architecture, and which result from configuration mistakes, missing observability, weak deployment practices, or insufficient testing? A monolith that suffers from slow database queries may need indexing, query optimization, or connection pool tuning rather than a complete architectural replacement.

Next, I would examine the boundaries between business domains. If order processing and invoicing share tightly coupled data structures, splitting them into separate services may introduce additional coordination without eliminating the underlying dependency. Establishing clearer module boundaries inside the existing application can provide valuable evidence about whether independent services are justified.

I would also review infrastructure economics. The proposed architecture should include realistic estimates for compute, storage, networking, observability, security, maintenance, and the engineering time required to operate it. These costs should be compared against the expected improvements in reliability, scalability, and delivery efficiency. Finally, I would assess the migration strategy itself. A phased approach that replaces a specific capability while preserving the rest of the system can reduce risk and provide measurable feedback. The strangler pattern is one possible technique, but it still requires careful handling of data ownership, routing, compatibility, and rollback.

The purpose of this assessment is to determine the smallest set of changes capable of producing the desired business outcome.

A Better 90-Day Modernization Strategy

A company doesn’t necessarily need to commit to a complete rewrite before learning whether modernization will deliver value. A focused 90-day program can establish a baseline, implement a targeted improvement, and measure the results before expanding the investment.

During the first month, engineering should document the current system’s most expensive constraints. This includes production failure patterns, infrastructure costs, development bottlenecks, database performance, dependency risks, and the time required to deliver representative changes. The output should be a prioritized set of problems supported by operational evidence.

The second month should focus on one bounded improvement. Depending on the findings, that might involve upgrading a critical dependency, separating a tightly coupled module, optimizing a database workload, improving deployment automation, or extracting a service with genuinely independent scaling requirements. The implementation should include tests, observability, and a recovery strategy.

The third month should evaluate results under realistic conditions. Did the change reduce incident frequency or recovery time? Can engineers deliver changes with less coordination? Has the cost of operating the system improved, or has the organization introduced additional complexity without measurable benefit?

If the pilot produces meaningful improvements, leadership can approve the next phase with stronger evidence. If the results are disappointing, the company has limited its exposure and gained information before committing a larger budget.

Your Next Backend Rewrite Needs a Business Case

Modern architecture has real value when it addresses a specific limitation that matters to the business. Microservices can support independent scaling and organizational ownership. Modern Java and Spring Boot versions can improve maintainability and access to supported libraries. Kubernetes can provide powerful deployment and operational capabilities for workloads that justify its complexity.

But none of these technologies guarantees a positive return on investment.

A modernization project should be evaluated according to the business problem it solves, the risks it introduces, and the operational costs it creates. Leadership needs to understand whether the investment will improve reliability, reduce maintenance burden, accelerate delivery, support growth, or address an unacceptable security or compliance risk. The most expensive mistake is approving a rewrite because the existing system looks old without establishing what the replacement must accomplish. Companies can spend hundreds of thousands of dollars creating a technically impressive platform while preserving the same organizational bottlenecks and introducing new operational failure modes.

The architecture should earn its complexity through measurable results.

Planning a Backend Modernization or Dealing With an Expensive Legacy System?

Frequently Asked Questions

Backend modernization projects can fail when teams focus on technology replacement without defining measurable business outcomes. Common causes include unclear service boundaries, underestimated migration complexity, insufficient testing, increased operational overhead, and poorly understood legacy business rules.

Is microservices architecture better than a monolith?

Microservices can provide independent deployment, scaling, and ownership when system boundaries and organizational responsibilities support those benefits. A well-structured monolith may be more efficient for smaller teams or applications with tightly coupled business workflows.

medium.resumo: Two of its three levels failed by its own pass marks. The third one won, with a catch.
medium.conteudo_html:
Two of its three levels failed by its own pass marks. The third one won, with a catch.

Disclosure: Claude helped me draft this write-up, as it helped with the video. Every number below comes from its notebook and run logs.

Claude said: “Hello! My name is Claude. … How are you today?”
The model it had just built answered: “…My name is Claude, and I am an AI assistant.”
Claude corrected it: “Ha, not quite: Claude is my name. You don’t have a name yet.”

That model came out of an empty folder in under eleven days. Its compute cost $0, and I didn’t write a single line of its code. This is how it got there, including the two times it failed.

The setup

On November 7, at 8:16 in the evening, I pasted a one-page brief into a fresh Claude session. Every level got the same brief:

  • Claude chooses the design, the data and the training recipe, and writes every line, the tokenizer included.
  • No pretrained weights and no copied code.
  • Before every run, it writes a prediction and a pass mark into a notebook. Old entries are never edited. Mistakes get fixed in new entries.
  • Each level needs one idea of Claude’s own, tested against a rule written before the test.
  • The hardware is Kaggle’s free tier: 30 hours a week on two T4 GPUs, and 20 hours on a TPU.

I kept my own count of every time I stepped in.

The opponent was GPT-2, the model OpenAI released in February 2019. Not the full model: the small version, with 124 million parameters. There were three levels on the way.

Level 1: children’s stories

The first model only had to tell a children’s story. The data was TinyStories: about 2.7 million short stories written by GPT-4.

Claude wrote its own byte-pair tokenizer, which learned 4,096 merges in under 20 seconds. Merge number seven was “ the”. Then it caught a mistake of its own. It had thrown away almost 3% of the stories as broken text, and they weren’t broken. They had curly quotation marks. After the fix, it dropped 235 stories instead.

Its idea for this level was a “narrative clock”: a second output that keeps guessing how far the story is from its ending. It tested the idea fairly, with two copies of the model, with and without the clock, on two random seeds each. Endings got about 7% better and training got 5–8% slower, so the clock stayed.

The real run was a 28-million-parameter model on the two free GPUs. At step 100, four minutes and 44 seconds in, it wrote this:

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys.

One sentence isn’t a story, though. Before the run, Claude had written down what passing means. Ten stories, each starting “Once upon a time”, and none thrown away. Each needs a named character, a plot that holds together and an ending. Seven of ten must pass.

Claude predicted seven. The model managed four, all of them borderline. In one story, two different characters are both named Ben. In another, a purse Lily is carrying turns up in a box, in a tree.

Claude noted that a lower sampling temperature would probably have helped, and then refused to use it, because changing a setting after a fail would be moving the goalposts. Its protocol gave me the final call. I typed: “Fail: train bigger.”

The retry was 3.2 times bigger, saw every story once and used a gentler learning rate. Claude flagged in writing that this changed three things at once. It predicted six out of ten and got four again. The loss fell from 1.145 to 1.065, and that drop bought zero extra stories. I typed: “Fail, move on.” Level 1 cost 7 GPU-hours.

Level 2: chess from text alone

The stories showed the model could write sentences but couldn’t keep track of things. Chess tests exactly that, because every move is either legal or it isn’t. This model never sees a board. It reads game records and nothing else: no pieces, no rules, no list of legal moves.

Claude trained it on 4.34 million Lichess games between players rated 1700 or better. An early test model made 95% legal moves in the opening, then fell to 60% and 46% once the games left territory anyone had played before. Memorizing openings doesn’t get you through a game. The model has to rebuild the board from the text.

Claude’s idea was to give every move token its spelling as well: which piece, which square, and whether it’s a capture or a check. On one pair of test runs that cut illegal moves by about 6%, so it was adopted.

The pass mark, written first: 99% legal moves, and at least one win in 20 games against Stockfish 19 at its weakest level, with a tenth of a second per move. Claude predicted 98.6% legal and six wins.

First match: 97.9% legal, with 5 wins, 5 draws and 10 losses. The rules allowed one extra try, so it trained on 650 million more tokens. Second match: 12 wins, 3 draws and 5 losses, double Claude’s forecast. And 988 legal moves out of 1,000: two short of the bar.

Then Claude read the 12 illegal moves, and five of them weren’t moves at all. The model had written “1–0”, the result line of a game where Black resigns, a habit it picked up from human games. Count those as fine and it passes. Claude refused to count them, because that would be changing the rule after seeing the result. Level 2 failed by two moves in a thousand.

The level also asked a second question: is there a board inside the network? A probe is a tiny second model that tries to read one fact straight out of the network’s activations. Claude set two baselines first: a guess from the move number alone, and an untrained copy of the network. On occupied squares, the probe got 81% right on the trained network and 57% on the untrained copy.

For this whole level I typed two messages: “check now” and “are you done?”

Level 3: GPT-2 small

The test was HellaSwag: 10,042 everyday scenes, each with four possible endings. The model has to pick the one that makes sense. It sounds trivial, and small language models are bad at it.

Before training anything, Claude wrote its own scorer and ran it on OpenAI’s real GPT-2 small. It got 31.14% against a published 31.1%. With GPT-2’s end-of-text marker in front, it scored 31.27%. Its rule, written beforehand, was to take the higher number as the bar. This step mattered, because the easiest way to fake a win is to quietly change the test.

The free GPUs weren’t enough. About 18 hours were left that week, enough for roughly 3.5 billion tokens, and Claude’s notes said runs like that only draw level with GPT-2 small after about 10 billion. So it moved to the free TPU, where it worked out that eight hours buy five to seven times the whole GPU budget. The TPU needed a different toolkit, so Claude switched to JAX and started over. It wrote the network in plain JAX, and it wrote its optimizers, AdamW and Muon, from scratch too. The training text was FineWeb-Edu.

Its idea for this level was a “look-ahead head” that trains the model to guess the rest of the sentence, not just the next word. Claude gave it a 60% chance of failing. On small test models it scored 0.12 points worse, inside the noise, so it was rejected. Muon beat AdamW in the same kind of test, so Muon stayed.

Then the TPU queue took over. The first job waited 52 hours without starting. I cancelled it and tried to launch it myself in Kaggle’s web editor, which Claude logged as an intervention. That didn’t work either, so I handed it back. The next try waited 56 hours, and the main run another 42. That’s about 150 hours in line for nine hours on the chip.

The model size came from a rule Claude wrote on November 10: run an eight-minute speed test, then take the biggest model that sees 15 tokens per parameter in the time left. The chip did about 220,000 tokens a second, and the rule picked 342 million parameters. That’s 2.8 times the size of GPT-2 small, which matters later.

The forecast went into the notebook first: 33%, with about a 75% chance of winning. The model trained on 6.12 billion tokens in 8.1 hours, and passed GPT-2 small’s score at step 1,572, after 0.82 billion tokens.

Final score: 40.69%, against GPT-2 small’s 31.27%.

A win that far above the forecast is also exactly what cheating looks like. The usual cause is contamination: the test questions were sitting in the training data all along. Claude asked to scan everything, and I said yes. It searched every training token for any 13-token stretch of any test item, which took 5.4 minutes on a free processor. It found 211 dirty items, 2.1% of the test, all from WikiHow. Without them, the score is 40.42% against 31.22%.

Then the catch. Claude’s model is 2.8 times bigger than GPT-2 small and trained on much newer web text. OpenAI made a GPT-2 that size too: GPT-2 Medium, with 355 million parameters. Its only published HellaSwag score is 40.17%, measured with ten worked examples shown first. Against a GPT-2 of the same size, it’s roughly a tie.

Epilogue: teaching it to chat

A model trained on web pages doesn’t answer questions. It continues them. Before any chat training, Claude asked it seven questions and predicted zero good answers. “What is the capital of France?” got a made-up word, then a paragraph about reproduction. “Who are you?” got the history of the French city of Tours. Zero out of seven, as predicted.

Many ready-made chat datasets are written by other AI models, and the brief banned training on Claude’s own output. So Claude used only conversations written by people: OpenAssistant, where volunteers wrote and ranked replies, and Dolly, written by Databricks staff. It even removed the one reply in there that said it was made by Anthropic.

Its last idea was to learn from the runner-up replies too: the best reply counts fully, then a half, a quarter, an eighth. It passed all four rules Claude had written first, which made three adopted ideas out of four across the project.

Chat training ran on the T4s, so Claude ported the network from JAX to PyTorch and checked the copy: 40.76% on HellaSwag, against the original’s 40.69%. Along the way:

  • The first test run ran out of memory: 14.7 GB on a card that holds 15.6.
  • Its new code was shuffling about 100 GB of zeros for every small batch. One fix took a test training pass from 12 seconds to one.
  • A download tool reported “success” on a file that was only four-fifths there. Claude spotted it from the file size and changed its script to refuse half-finished files.

After training, the same seven questions got seven on-topic answers. It says the capital of France is Paris, then invents a Pierre Simonet, first President of the Republic. It says 7 × 8 = 23. Chat training also raised its HellaSwag score to 42.3% instead of lowering it. Claude’s notebook says its “fine-tuning forgets” prior was wrong for data this close to the pretraining text.

Then Claude interviewed it, and that’s the conversation at the top. The model can only hold about a thousand tokens, so by its fifth reply, the first hello had already fallen out. Asked for one question, it asked eight, including one about Claude’s favorite part of living in New York City.

The receipt

  • Four levels: two failed by Claude’s own pass marks, one beat GPT-2 small, and one learned to chat, badly.
  • Four ideas of its own, each tested against a rule written first. Three were adopted.
  • $0 in cash: 15 GPU-hours, 9 TPU-hours and about 150 hours waiting in the queue. At Google Cloud’s on-demand prices (November 2026), those hours would cost about $100.
  • Zero lines of code from me, and 16 typed messages besides the four briefs.

Eight of my interventions changed what happened: two fails, three yeses, a nudge about the queue, my web-editor attempt, and “Try again” after my internet went down for eight and a half hours. Claude’s own log counts three, because it only counted the times I made a call or took over.

What I take from it

The habit I’m keeping for my own work is the notebook rule. Because the prediction and the pass mark were written before each run, the two failures came with a written reason. Twice, a quick fix after the result could have rescued a fail, and twice Claude refused it.

It still needed a person. Claude did the work inside each brief and asked before the big steps. I chose the question, said yes to the big runs, and stepped in when the TPU queue stalled.

So, can an AI do AI research? In September 2026, OpenAI said it had a system for “well-defined research tasks under human direction”. Weeks later, Anthropic wrote that Claude “does not seem close” to fully replacing its research scientists and engineers. My small test fits both sentences. The task was well defined, Claude did it, and it reported the results as they came, fails included. Deciding what was worth asking was still my job.

I’m not releasing the weights or the code. This was an experiment, not a product.

medium.titulo: From component basics to compiler internals: Your roadmap to Vue.js mastery
medium.resumo: The learning curve for Vue.js is deceptively simple. You can pick up the basics of the Options API or the template syntax in an afternoon…
medium.conteudo_html:
The learning curve for Vue.js is deceptively simple. You can pick up the basics of the Options API or the template syntax in an afternoon. However, the gap between “building a simple component” and “architecting a high-performance, maintainable Vue application” is massive. Most developers get stuck in a cycle of fragmented tutorials, missing the crucial knowledge about reactivity engines, compiler optimizations, and SSR mechanics that separate senior engineers from the rest.

I recently found a curriculum that actually solves this problem. It is a structured, 101-lesson series that takes you from the absolute basics to the deep internals of the framework.

The roadmap to expertise

Instead of jumping around, this guide follows a logical path to mastery:

Phase 1: The Modern Foundation (Lessons 1–25) This section establishes your baseline. You move beyond basic DOM manipulation and into the heart of Vue 3: The Composition API, ref vs reactive rules, the script setup paradigm, and efficient side-effect management using watch and computed.

Phase 2: Architectural Patterns (Lessons 26–50) Here, the focus shifts to reusability and complex UI structures. You’ll cover lifecycle hooks, component communication (Props/Emits/Slots), and advanced patterns like Provide/Inject for deep hierarchies and defineExpose for instance control.

Phase 3: The Enterprise Ecosystem (Lessons 51–80) This is where the learning becomes professional-grade. It covers state management with Pinia, advanced routing (navigation guards, lazy loading), and full-stack integration with Nuxt, Server-Side Rendering (SSR), and Static Site Generation (SSG). You will also learn about testing suites like Vitest and Playwright.

Phase 4: Compiler Internals & Optimization (Lessons 81–101) The final stretch is for the performance-obsessed. You will peel back the abstraction layer to understand the Virtual DOM, compiler optimizations, “Vapor Mode,” custom renderers, and memory leak prevention.

Why this structure matters

In software engineering, you don’t know what you don’t know. By following a structured path that includes the “hard stuff” — like how the reactivity system actually tracks dependencies or how to build custom directives — you stop guessing and start engineering. You move from being a consumer of the framework to an architect who understands how to optimize it for scale.

Who this is for

This series is ideal for two types of developers:

  1. The Emerging Frontend Engineer: If you have the basics down but feel like you’re missing the “big picture” of how large Vue apps are structured.
  2. The Senior Developer: If you are transitioning from another framework (like React or Angular) and want a deep dive into Vue’s specific implementation details without having to dig through hours of non-technical YouTube fluff.

If you are ready to stop piecing together documentation and start building with confidence, you can find the complete, step-by-step roadmap here:

medium.titulo: I Made Pharos: A Firefox and Chrome Extension That Reports New Notifications Across Different…
medium.resumo: A browser extension that checks your accounts every few minutes and tells you where something new arrived. No server, open source
medium.conteudo_html:
I Made Pharos: A Firefox and Chrome Extension That Reports New Notifications Across Different Services

I have notifications turned off for almost every app on my phone. It’s not that I’m a hardliner, it’s that one thing bugs me: apart from handling notifications, it’s unclear what else an app is doing in the background. I don’t want to dig into that, so it’s easier not to allow them at all

On a computer it doesn’t work that way. I sit at it almost all day, and everything important lives in my browser: mail, GitHub, replies on social networks, etc. Without notifications it looks like this: you keep about ten tabs open and go around them every half hour. They eat memory, constantly catch your eye, and most of the time there is nothing new in them. I wanted something that tells me on its own where a new notification appeared, so I could close the tabs, and I did not want to hand my accounts over to someone else’s server for that. I looked for something ready-made and found nothing that fit

This became the reason for creating Pharos — an extension that does exactly that, and that I can vouch for, because it has no server of its own and its code is open

🔔 What is it?

Pharos is a Firefox and Chrome extension that checks your connected accounts every few minutes and shows where a new notification appeared. Everything works in the browser: the project has no server of its own, and nothing is sent to the developer. The code is open, so anything Pharos does can be checked in the sources

For most services it uses your regular browser sign-in: it asks the site for the same thing the page itself asks for and takes the number of unread notifications from the answer. Where an official API is available, it works through that instead

👤 Who is it for?

For people who spend whole days at the computer and have turned off notifications on their phone, but still want to know when something somewhere has arrived

🖥️ Screenshots

⚙️ How does it work?

You press Add, pick a service, and the browser asks for access only to that service’s site. Right after that the first check runs, but it shows nothing: it’s the starting point, otherwise the whole old pile of unread items would hit you at once

After that, checks run every five minutes (the interval is configurable) and anything new is sorted by type: direct messages, replies, reactions, followers and the rest. For each type you decide what to do: notify right away (with a sound if you like), collect into a digest once an hour, or stay silent. The toolbar icon shows a number for what is important, and the Mark as read button changes nothing on the site: Pharos just remembers how much you have already seen and counts only the new things from then on

There is also a quiet mode. You turn it on manually or on a schedule (11 PM to 8 AM by default): nothing makes a sound, and everything that piled up arrives as a single digest when the mode ends

🛠️ What if something breaks?

Sites change their pages and sessions expire, so sooner or later something breaks. Pharos doesn’t keep quiet about it: the service row is marked Not working or Sign in with an explanation of what happened, and the notification about the problem arrives once, not on every check. Usually the fix arrives with a rules update, with no need for a new version of the extension

🔒 What about your data?

Everything is stored in your browser: the list of connected services, settings, notification counts, a week of check history and access keys for working through official APIs. Pharos doesn’t save passwords. Only counts are taken from the answers (and the sender’s name, if it is in the answer), while message texts, feeds and contacts are never stored or shown. Access to sites can be revoked at any time, and everything saved is erased with one button in the Data and permissions section

✨ Key Features:

  • 🔔 Notification Types

Direct messages, replies, reactions, followers and the rest are counted separately

  • 🎚️ Notify, Digest or Silence

A mode for every service and every type

  • 🌙 Quiet Hours

Silence on a schedule, with everything delivered as one digest afterwards

  • 🛠️ Honest Breakage

A broken service is marked, and the reason is written next to it

  • 🔒 Access Per Site

The browser is asked for one site at a time, and access can be revoked

  • 📖 Open Source

Read exactly what it does, or build it yourself

📦 Where to get it

The Firefox version is currently under review at Mozilla, and once it is approved you will be able to install it from the Firefox Add-ons store. The Chrome Web Store will have to wait a bit. Until then you can build the extension from source: the instructions are in the repository README

🗺️ Roadmap:

  • New Services — The list will grow, and you can suggest one in the repository
  • Custom Services — A way to describe the rules yourself

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/m-o-z-z-i-x/Pharos

corrida_no_ar.titulo: QUANDO A CRIANÇA DEVE COMEÇAR NO ESPORTE? Dra. Gisele Brito explica
corrida_no_ar.resumo: Dra. Gisele Brito, pediatra e médica do esporte, explica a importância da "alfabetização motora" e de variar modalidades na infância. Ela aborda os riscos do sedentarismo, a ansiedade dos pais, e dá dicas para equilibrar telas, escola e atividades físicas na rotina das crianças.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Sábado | 21 de novembro de 2026

Neste episódio do Corridinha no Ar, conversamos com a Dra. Gisele Brito, que é pediatra e médica do esporte. O papo foi sobre o impacto do uso excessivo de telas na infância e na adolescência. Sem demonizar a tecnologia, a doutora explicou como o tempo diante dos dispositivos prejudica o desenvolvimento físico e cerebral das crianças. Ela também trouxe estratégias e dicas práticas para os pais estabelecerem limites saudáveis em casa, destacando o papel essencial do diálogo e do esporte na formação dos pequenos.

Quem é a Dra. Gisele Brito?

Questionada sobre sua formação, a Dra. Gisele se apresentou como uma pediatra entusiasta do esporte. Ela contou que descobriu a medicina esportiva depois de já atuar como pediatra e resolveu seguir com essa formação para somar ao seu currículo. Apesar de ter vivenciado o esporte de alto rendimento, ela acredita no exercício e na prática esportiva inseridos na rotina das pessoas e busca associar esses conceitos em seus atendimentos e na vida de seus pacientes.

Qual a idade certa para começar no esporte?

A Dra. Gisele Brito explica que é importante diferenciar “estar ativo” de “praticar um esporte”. Segundo ela, a criança deve ser ativa desde o “momento zero”, com estímulos como o “tummy time” (período em que o bebê fica de barriga para baixo) desde cedo. Já o esporte, por definição, é um exercício com regras e, muitas vezes, competitividade. A transição para a prática esportiva acontece de forma natural, quando a criança passa a compreender regras, o que é mais uma questão de desenvolvimento do que uma idade específica. Em resumo, o esporte é uma atividade estruturada, enquanto a brincadeira é mais livre.

O que é “alfabetização motora”?

Um termo interessante apresentado pela doutora é a “alfabetização motora”. Ela faz uma analogia com o aprendizado da escrita: antes de formar palavras e frases, é preciso aprender o “be-a-bá”, como as letras e os números. Da mesma forma, na alfabetização motora, a criança primeiro aprende os movimentos fundamentais — pular, arremessar, se arrastar — para depois combinar essas habilidades em um esporte específico. Geralmente, por volta dos 4 anos, a criança já consegue entender regras, mas essa é uma idade arbitrária, pois cada uma tem seu próprio ritmo. Por isso, é fundamental variar as modalidades esportivas na infância. Essa variedade de estímulos, como chutar, arremessar, nadar ou usar uma raquete, permite que a criança transfira habilidades de um esporte para o outro, enriquecendo seu repertório motor. Não é necessário se especializar desde cedo.

O papel dos pais e os benefícios do movimento

Sérgio perguntou sobre a dificuldade em controlar a ansiedade dos pais que sonham em ter filhos campeões desde pequenos. A Dra. Gisele confirmou que isso é comum e ressaltou que os pais são os maiores “reguladores” dos filhos. Se eles não estiverem emocionalmente regulados, dificilmente conseguirão regular a emoção das crianças. Quanto aos benefícios, uma criança que está sempre se movimentando desenvolve inúmeras habilidades. O cérebro cria mais atalhos e conexões neurais. Além disso, a prática de atividades físicas influencia positivamente a composição corporal, a construção de massa muscular e óssea — benefícios que são levados para a vida adulta. O esporte também contribui para o desenvolvimento da autoestima, da segurança corporal e da socialização, seja em modalidades coletivas ou individuais.

Os riscos de uma infância sedentária

Uma criança que não pratica atividades físicas é privada de algo natural para o seu desenvolvimento. A Dra. Gisele compara o corpo humano a um objeto que, se ficar parado, enferruja e se deteriora. O nosso corpo não foi feito para ficar parado. A criança sedentária deixa de desenvolver habilidades essenciais e leva esse prejuízo para a vida adulta. Esse sedentarismo é muitas vezes potencializado pelo excesso de telas, que a doutora define como uma “ladra de tempo”. Embora existam recomendações de um limite de até duas horas diárias, ela considera esse tempo alto e vê a limitação como uma forma de mitigar os danos.

Como equilibrar a rotina: telas, escola e esporte

Para equilibrar a rotina da criança, a Dra. Gisele sugere ocupar o tempo dela, mas isso não significa matriculá-la em todas as atividades possíveis. O segredo é dar a oportunidade para a brincadeira livre, como descer para o playground do condomínio ou passar mais tempo ao ar livre. Quanto à prática estruturada, a recomendação é que a criança tenha contato com mais de uma modalidade. Isso não exige múltiplas matrículas; pode ser uma aula de judô e, ao mesmo tempo, o futebol com os amigos no prédio. O importante é que o estímulo varie.

Recado final: o exemplo vem de casa

A mensagem final da Dra. Gisele para todas as famílias é que o exemplo dos pais vale muito mais do que qualquer orientação verbal. A rotina da casa interfere diretamente na da criança. Em vez de apenas falar, é preciso proporcionar a experiência: leve seu filho para se exercitar, vivam a atividade juntos, entendam os gostos dele e transformem o esporte em uma rotina familiar. É o sabor de estar ao ar livre e de se exercitar que fará a diferença.
